lessons.title: Market Structure Basics — Reading the Chart
lessons.subtitle: Higher Highs, Higher Lows & the Language of Price

steps.text: Market structure is the foundational concept in SMC. It refers to the sequence of highs and lows that price creates as it moves across a chart. By analyzing these swing points, you can determine whether the market is trending up, trending down, or ranging. Institutional traders rely on structure to decide their bias before placing a single trade. Without understanding market structure, you are trading blind. Think of structure as the roadmap that tells you where price has been and where it is likely to go next. Every decision you make as a trader should be filtered through the lens of market structure first.

An uptrend is defined by a sequence of Higher Highs and Higher Lows. Each successive peak is higher than the previous peak, and each successive trough is higher than the previous trough. This pattern tells you that buying pressure exceeds selling pressure over time. Institutions are accumulating positions during this phase, driving price higher. As a trader, your bias in an uptrend should be to look for buying opportunities only. The moment you see a Higher Low form after a pullback, that is your confirmation that the uptrend remains intact and you can consider a long entry.

A downtrend is the mirror image of an uptrend. It is characterized by Lower Highs and Lower Lows, meaning each rally fails to exceed the previous high and each decline breaks below the previous low. This structure indicates that sellers are in full control. Institutions are distributing their positions, and retail traders who try to catch bottoms get crushed. In a downtrend, your bias must be bearish. Wait for a Lower High to form, then look for short entries. Fighting the trend is the fastest way to lose money in the markets.

Exercise: Identify the structure. Price makes a high at 1.1050, drops to 1.0900, rallies to 1.1080, drops to 1.0920, rallies to 1.1120, drops to 1.0950. Is this an uptrend, downtrend, or ranging market? Look at the highs: 1.1050, 1.1080, 1.1120 — each is higher. Lows: 1.0900, 1.0920, 1.0950 — each is higher. This is a clear uptrend with Higher Highs and Higher Lows. Your bias should be bullish.

Not all markets trend. In a ranging market, price oscillates between a defined support and resistance zone without making clear Higher Highs or Lower Lows. The highs are roughly equal, and the lows are roughly equal. This is also called a consolidation phase. Institutions use ranging markets to accumulate or distribute positions before the next big move. For a trader, ranging markets are dangerous because false breakouts are common. The best approach is to wait for price to break out of the range with conviction and then trade the breakout or the return to the range boundary.

To draw market structure manually, start from the left side of your chart and identify the most recent significant swing high and swing low. A swing high is a candlestick with lower highs on both sides, and a swing low is a candlestick with higher lows on both sides. Connect these swing points with horizontal lines to mark key levels. Then draw diagonal lines connecting the sequence of Higher Highs and Higher Lows for an uptrend, or Lower Highs and Lower Lows for a downtrend. Always use the higher timeframe for your primary structure analysis and drop down to lower timeframes for entries.

Institutions manage enormous capital and cannot enter or exit positions like retail traders can. They need significant liquidity to fill their orders, which is why they respect structural levels. When price approaches a previous high or low, institutions watch to see if the level will hold or break. If it holds, they use it as a support or resistance zone to enter positions. If it breaks, they use the break as confirmation of a trend change. This respect for structure is what makes technical analysis work — institutions create the patterns that smart traders learn to recognize.

Consider EUR/USD on the 4-hour chart. Price formed a low at 1.0900, rallied to 1.1050, pulled back to 1.0950, then rallied to 1.1120, pulled back to 1.1000, and rallied again to 1.1250. This is a textbook uptrend. Notice how each pullback found buyers at a higher level than the previous one. A trader following SMC would look to buy at each Higher Low with a stop below the previous swing low, targeting the next swing high. This is structure-based trading in action — letting the market tell you where to enter.

The most common mistake beginners make is drawing structure on too low a timeframe, seeing noise instead of meaningful swings. Another major mistake is redrawing structure to fit a desired bias, such as ignoring a Lower High because you want to stay bullish. Beginners also confuse a pullback with a trend reversal — a single Lower Low does not make a downtrend if the overall sequence of Higher Highs remains intact. Finally, many traders fail to wait for confirmation: they enter before a Higher Low has been confirmed by the next candle. Patience is king in structure trading.

Final exercise: A chart shows High = 100, Low = 90, High = 105, Low = 92, High = 103, Low = 88. What is the structure? Highs: 100 to 105 to 103. Lows: 90 to 92 to 88. The last high at 103 is lower than 105, and the last low at 88 is lower than 92. This is a shift: we have a Lower High and a Lower Low, indicating a potential trend change from uptrend to downtrend. Your bias should shift from bullish to bearish. Never trade against the current structure.

lessons.title: Understanding Liquidity — Where the Banks Hide
lessons.subtitle: Buy-Side & Sell-Side Liquidity Explained

steps.text: In trading, liquidity refers to the volume of pending orders waiting to be executed at specific price levels. These are stop-losses, take-profits, and limit orders placed by retail traders. For institutional traders, liquidity is the fuel they need to enter or exit large positions without moving the market against themselves. Without sufficient liquidity, a bank cannot fill a multi-million dollar order. Understanding where liquidity sits is the single most important skill in SMC because it tells you where price is likely to go next — banks go where the liquidity is.

Buy-side liquidity sits above old highs. When price breaks above a previous high, it triggers the stop-losses of traders who sold short at that level. Those stop-losses are buy orders, which provide the liquidity institutions need to sell their long positions into. Think of it this way: if you are a bank holding a massive long position and you want to exit at a profit, you need buyers. Where do you find buyers? Above the old high, where trapped short-sellers are forced to buy back. This is why price often spikes above old highs before reversing down.

Sell-side liquidity sits below old lows. When price breaks below a previous low, it triggers the stop-losses of traders who bought long at that level. Those stop-losses are sell orders, which provide the liquidity institutions need to buy their short positions back. If a bank is short and wants to cover, they need sellers. Where do they find sellers? Below the old low, where trapped longs are forced to sell. This is why price often spikes below old lows before reversing up. Every old high and low is a potential liquidity pool.

Institutions need liquidity because their orders are massive. When a hedge fund wants to sell 10,000 lots of EUR/USD, they cannot just place a market order — that would crash the price. Instead, they need to find enough buyers to absorb their sell order. The most efficient place to find those buyers is above a previous high, where stop-losses from short-sellers are clustered. This is why price moves from liquidity pool to liquidity pool. The entire movement of the market can be understood as a hunt for liquidity. Without this concept, chart patterns seem random.

The liquidity grab works in a specific sequence. Step 1: Price approaches a key level (an old high or low). Step 2: Retail traders place their stops just beyond that level. Step 3: Institutions drive price beyond the level, triggering all those stops. Step 4: The stops provide the liquidity the institution needs. Step 5: Price reverses sharply in the true direction. This is often called a stop hunt or liquidity sweep. Recognizing this pattern allows you to avoid being the liquidity and instead position yourself to ride the institutional move that follows.

Double tops and double bottoms are classic liquidity traps. In a double top, price rallies to a previous high, pulls back, then rallies again to the same level. Most retail traders see this as a resistance level and sell short, placing their stops above the high. Institutions know this and push price just above the high to grab those stops, then reverse hard to the downside. The same happens with double bottoms in reverse. Never trade a double top or bottom as a simple reversal; wait to see if it becomes a liquidity grab first.

Practice: On a chart, identify the most recent swing high and the most recent swing low. Mark a horizontal line at each level. These are your primary liquidity zones. Now consider: if price approaches the high from below, where are the stop-losses of short-sellers? Above the high. If price approaches the low from above, where are the stop-losses of long traders? Below the low. Label these as buy-side liquidity (above highs) and sell-side liquidity (below lows). This is how you map liquidity on any chart before taking a trade.

Consider XAU/USD (Gold) on the 1-hour chart. Price formed a low at $2,620 and rallied to $2,680. It then pulled back to $2,650, rallied again to $2,685, and pulled back to $2,660. Many traders sold at $2,680 expecting a double top, placing stops above $2,685. Suddenly, price spiked to $2,692, grabbing all those stops, then reversed sharply down to $2,630 in the next few hours. This is a textbook liquidity grab. The spike above $2,685 was the hunt, and the move down was the real direction. Identifying this pattern would have saved you from being trapped.

Before taking any trade, you should map liquidity on your chart. Start with the daily timeframe: mark the most recent swing high and swing low. Then move to the 4-hour chart: mark the relevant highs and lows within the daily range. Finally, on the 1-hour chart, identify the immediate liquidity levels near current price. Your trade plan should include: where is the liquidity above (for potential shorts) and where is the liquidity below (for potential longs). Never enter a trade without knowing where the nearest liquidity sits, because that is where price is likely heading.

Most retail traders lose money because they fail to understand liquidity. When a retail trader places a stop-loss just above a high or below a low, they are placing their money directly in the path of institutional algorithms designed to hunt those exact levels. The solution is not to stop using stop-losses, but to place them at levels where they are less likely to be targeted, or to use wider stops beyond the obvious liquidity zone. Understanding liquidity transforms you from prey into a trader who can anticipate where price will move next. Respect liquidity or become liquidity.

lessons.title: Break of Structure & Change of Character
lessons.subtitle: BOS — The Market Confirms, CHoCH — The Market Reverses

steps.text: Break of Structure (BOS) is a continuation signal. It occurs when price breaks beyond a structural level in the direction of the current trend. In an uptrend, a BOS happens when price breaks above the previous Higher High. In a downtrend, a BOS happens when price breaks below the previous Lower Low. A BOS confirms that the trend is still alive and that institutions are continuing to push price in the trending direction. When you see a BOS, it tells you that your current bias is correct and that you should continue looking for entries in the same direction.

Change of Character (CHoCH) is a potential reversal signal. It occurs when price breaks a structural level against the current trend. In an uptrend, a CHoCH happens when price breaks below the previous Higher Low, creating a Lower Low. In a downtrend, a CHoCH happens when price breaks above the previous Lower High, creating a Higher High. CHoCH tells you that the current trend may be ending and a new trend may be starting. It is your alert to stop trading in the old direction and start preparing for the new direction.

Visualize this on a real chart: In an uptrend, price makes HH at 1.1200, HL at 1.1100, HH at 1.1300, HL at 1.1150, HH at 1.1400. Then price drops to 1.1050, breaking below the previous HL at 1.1100. That break below 1.1100 is a CHoCH. The market has shown it can no longer maintain Higher Lows. The trend character has changed from bullish to potentially bearish. In contrast, if from the HL at 1.1100 price rallies to 1.1350 (above 1.1300), that is a BOS — the uptrend continues. Knowing this distinction is critical because it determines whether you should buy or sell.

To confirm a CHoCH, you need more than just a single break. A valid CHoCH requires that the previous structural level is clearly broken with momentum. Look for a strong candlestick close beyond the level, not just a wick that pierces it. Additionally, the CHoCH should be preceded by a liquidity grab — a sweep of the old high (in an uptrend) or old low (in a downtrend). The sequence is: liquidity grab at a key level, then a break of the opposite structural level. When both conditions are met, the CHoCH is confirmed and you can act on it with confidence.

The relationship between liquidity grab and CHoCH is fundamental in SMC. Consider an uptrend: price rallies to an old high, grabs liquidity above it (stop hunt), then reverses and breaks the last Higher Low. The liquidity grab was the trap, and the CHoCH is the confirmation. This is the typical reversal pattern in SMC. Without the liquidity grab first, a CHoCH is less reliable because there may not be enough institutional interest to sustain the reversal. Always look for a liquidity grab before a CHoCH. This two-step sequence is the bread and butter of institutional reversal trading.

When trading with BOS, the most reliable approach is to wait for a second BOS before entering. The first BOS confirms the trend is alive, and the second BOS confirms that momentum is continuing. After the first BOS, wait for a pullback to form an Order Block or FVG on the lower timeframe, then enter when price breaks the structure again. This second BOS entry filters out false breakouts and weak moves. For example, in a downtrend, wait for price to break below the first LL, pull back to an OB, then enter short on the break below the next low.

A CHoCH is your alert to stop trading the old direction. If you are in a long trade and you see a CHoCH against you, it is a warning that the trend may be ending. At minimum, you should tighten your stop-loss or take partial profits. If you are looking for new trades and you see a CHoCH, stop looking for entries in the old trend direction and start looking for entries in the new direction. Many traders lose money because they ignore a CHoCH and continue buying into a market that has already turned. The CHoCH is the market speaking — listen to it.

Warning: Not every break of a level is a true CHoCH. Sometimes price breaks a low but immediately reverses back above it — this is a fake CHoCH, also known as a retracement trap. A true CHoCH has follow-through: after breaking the level, price continues in the new direction and does not return above the broken level. A fake CHoCH occurs when institutions shake out weak hands before continuing the original trend. To distinguish them, wait for a retest of the broken level. If the level holds as new support or resistance, the CHoCH is valid. If price crosses back, it was a fake.

Multiple timeframe confirmation is essential when trading BOS and CHoCH. Always check the higher timeframe to ensure your BOS or CHoCH aligns with the larger trend. A CHoCH on the 15-minute chart may be just a pullback within the 4-hour uptrend. Conversely, a CHoCH on the daily chart is a major event that should not be ignored. The rule: trade in the direction of the higher timeframe trend, and use BOS and CHoCH on the lower timeframe for entries. When the higher and lower timeframes align, your trade has the highest probability of success.

Build your structure-based trading plan. Step 1: Identify the trend on the daily chart using HH/HL or LH/LL. Step 2: On the 4-hour chart, mark key liquidity levels. Step 3: Wait for a liquidity grab at a key level. Step 4: Watch for a CHoCH confirming a reversal or a BOS confirming continuation. Step 5: Enter in the direction of the confirmed structure. Write this plan down and follow it for every trade. A written plan forces discipline and prevents emotional decisions. Review your plan after every trade to see where you deviated.

lessons.title: Fair Value Gaps — The Market's Inefficiency
lessons.subtitle: FVG: When Price Moves Too Fast

steps.text: A Fair Value Gap (FVG) is created when price moves so aggressively in one direction that it leaves a gap on the chart where little to no trading occurred. This happens when institutions place a massive market order that consumes all available orders at multiple price levels instantly. The result is a three-candle formation where the wicks of the surrounding candles do not fully overlap, leaving an empty zone in between. This empty zone represents price levels that the market skipped over, creating an inefficiency that price often returns to fill.

The anatomy of an FVG consists of three consecutive candles. Candle 1: A regular candle that establishes the starting point. Candle 2: An aggressive candle with a large body and small wicks, moving strongly in one direction. Candle 3: A candle that continues in the same direction or holds the move. The FVG is the gap between the wick of Candle 1 and the wick of Candle 3. For a bullish FVG, you look at the area between the low of Candle 3 and the high of Candle 1. For a bearish FVG, it is between the high of Candle 3 and the low of Candle 1.

Bullish and Bearish FVGs are mirror images. A bullish FVG forms during an aggressive upward move, leaving a gap between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3 that represents unfilled buy orders. Price typically returns to this zone before continuing higher. A bearish FVG forms during an aggressive downward move, leaving a gap between the low of candle 1 and the high of candle 3 that represents unfilled sell orders. Price returns to fill this gap before resuming the downtrend. The direction of the FVG tells you the direction of institutional interest.

To identify FVGs on any timeframe: look for three consecutive candles where the second candle has an unusually large body compared to those around it. Check if the wick of candle 1 overlaps with the wick of candle 3. If there is a space between them, you have found an FVG. Draw a rectangle between the non-overlapping wicks. This rectangle marks the inefficiency zone. Practice on a 1-hour EUR/USD chart: scan from left to right and mark every FVG you find. You will be surprised how frequently they appear, especially around news events and session opens.

FVG mitigation refers to the process of price returning to fill the inefficiency gap. The market seeks balance, so it tends to revisit these gaps to fill unfilled orders. When price returns to an FVG, it is said to be mitigating the gap. This is your trading opportunity. If price enters the FVG and immediately reverses, the gap has acted as support or resistance and you can enter in the direction of the original move. If price passes through the FVG completely, the gap has been filled and is no longer relevant. Mitigation is the key event that turns an FVG into a tradeable zone.

Trading FVG mitigation is straightforward. Identify a bullish FVG in an uptrend. Wait for price to pull back and enter the FVG zone. Look for confirmation of the reversal within the gap, such as a bullish candlestick pattern like a hammer or a strong bullish engulfing candle. Enter long with a stop-loss below the FVG. Target the next liquidity zone above the most recent high. For a bearish FVG in a downtrend, wait for price to rally into the gap, confirm with a bearish candlestick, enter short, stop above the gap, and target the next low. Always confirm the reversal within the gap before entering.

An FVG can also act as support or resistance if price does not fully mitigate it. If price enters the FVG, touches one edge, and reverses without filling the entire gap, that edge becomes a significant level. This is called a partial mitigation. For example, price enters a bullish FVG from below, touches the upper boundary, and reverses up. The upper boundary now acts as support. You can place a buy stop above that level or enter on a retest. Partial mitigations are often more powerful than full mitigations because they show strong institutional defense of that zone.

Inversion occurs when price breaks through an FVG completely without reversing. If price enters a bullish FVG and continues downward through the entire gap, the FVG is considered invalidated and inverted. The gap that was once support becomes resistance. This is important because many traders enter expecting the gap to hold, and when it breaks, they get trapped. If you see price slicing through an FVG without a reversal, do not fight it. The institutional move was stronger than expected, and price is heading further in that direction. An inverted FVG tells you the trend may have shifted.

Combining FVG with Order Blocks creates powerful confluence zones. An Order Block (OB) is the last candle before the FVG formed. When the OB and FVG overlap at the same price level, you have a high-probability trade zone. The OB represents where institutions placed their orders, and the FVG represents the aggressive execution of those orders. Together, they form a zone of strong institutional interest. When price returns to this combined zone, the probability of a reversal is much higher than with either factor alone. Always look for OB+FVG confluences when planning your entries.

Practical exercise: Open a 15-minute chart of GBP/USD. Scroll back through the last 24 hours of price action. Identify every three-candle sequence where a large-bodied candle created a gap between the wicks of the surrounding candles. Mark them as bullish (gap above, price went up) or bearish (gap below, price went down). Then check which gaps have been mitigated and which are still open. For the unmitigated gaps, note the price level — price may return to fill them. This exercise trains your eye to spot FVGs quickly and naturally.

lessons.title: Order Blocks — The Institutional Footprint
lessons.subtitle: Finding Where Smart Money Left Their Orders

steps.text: An Order Block (OB) is a specific candlestick or group of candlesticks where institutions placed their large pending orders before a significant move. In SMC, a bullish Order Block is the last down-candle immediately before an aggressive up-move. A bearish Order Block is the last up-candle immediately before an aggressive down-move. Think of the OB as the launchpad: it is the price level where smart money decided to commit their capital. When price returns to this level, institutions will defend it because they still have orders there.

To identify a bullish Order Block: look for a down-candle (red or bearish) that is immediately followed by a strong up-move that breaks above the recent structure. The bullish OB is typically the last bearish candle before price starts rallying aggressively. Its low often acts as the invalidation point for the move. The candle may have a long wick to the downside, showing that institutions collected sell-side liquidity there before reversing. The larger the down-candle relative to surrounding candles, the more significant the OB tends to be.

To identify a bearish Order Block: look for an up-candle (green or bullish) that is immediately followed by a strong down-move that breaks below recent structure. The bearish OB is the last bullish candle before the sell-off begins. Its high often acts as the invalidation point. The candle may have a long wick to the upside, indicating collection of buy-side liquidity. The strength of the OB is proportional to the strength of the move that follows it. A massive bearish candle following a small bullish OB tells you that institutional selling was aggressive.

Order Blocks differ from regular support and resistance because they are not arbitrary round numbers or trend lines. An OB is specifically tied to institutional order flow and has a clear cause-and-effect relationship with the subsequent price move. While regular support levels are subjective (different traders draw them differently), an OB is objective — it is the last candle before the move. Additionally, OBs have a defined invalidation point: if price breaks through the OB candle's low (for bullish) or high (for bearish), the OB is no longer valid and the trade setup is void.

Not all OBs are equally useful. A fresh OB is one that price has not yet returned to test. It is still active and likely to be respected when price returns. A used OB is one that price has already visited and reversed from — it has been partially or fully mitigated and is less likely to hold again. When scanning for OBs, prioritize fresh blocks that formed on the higher timeframe (4H or Daily) with a strong subsequent move. These are the OBs that institutions are most likely to defend. Avoid OBs that have already been tested multiple times, as they tend to lose their significance.

OB mitigation is similar to FVG mitigation: price returns to the Order Block zone to test if institutions still have orders there. When price reaches the OB, you will see a reaction — either a bounce (the OB holds) or a break (the OB fails). The bounce is your entry signal. For a bullish OB, wait for price to come down into the block, show a reversal candle (like a hammer or bullish engulfing), then enter long. For a bearish OB, wait for price to rally into the block, show a bearish reversal candle (shooting star or bearish engulfing), then enter short.

When trading with Order Blocks, the structure is clear. Entry: enter on the confirmation candle after price reaches the OB. Stop-loss: place it just below the bullish OB low (for longs) or just above the bearish OB high (for shorts). This placement ensures that if the OB is invalidated, you are out of the trade with a small loss. Take-profit: target the next significant liquidity zone. For a long, target the next high. For a short, target the next low. The risk-reward ratio should be at least 1:2. If the distance from entry to stop is larger than half the distance to the target, the trade is not worth taking.

The OB+FVG confluence is one of the most reliable setups in SMC. When an Order Block and a Fair Value Gap exist at the same price level, you have multiple institutional fingerprints pointing to the same zone. The OB tells you where orders were placed, and the FVG tells you that the market moved too fast through that area. When price returns to this convergence zone, three outcomes are possible: the zone acts as support/resistance and price reverses, the zone holds with a small wick through, or the zone breaks completely. The probability of a reversal is highest when both align perfectly.

Consider GBP/USD on the weekly chart. In early 2024, price formed a clear bullish Order Block at 1.2500 — the last down-candle before a 400-pip rally to 1.2900. Months later, price pulled back to retest the 1.2500 zone. Many traders expected it to break because the level was months old. But the OB held perfectly, and price bounced 300 pips higher. This is the power of Order Blocks on higher timeframes: they can remain relevant for weeks or even months because institutions leave standing orders that do not expire quickly. Trust the OB, especially on weekly and daily charts.

The psychology behind why OBs work is simple. When a large institution decides to enter a massive position, they cannot fill it all at once. They place multiple layers of orders at different price levels. The Order Block represents the first layer of those orders. When price returns to the OB, more of those institutional orders are waiting to be filled, creating a natural floor or ceiling. Retail traders see the OB as a good entry point because they know institutions will defend it. This collective awareness makes OBs self-fulfilling to some degree, but their primary power comes from actual institutional order flow.

lessons.title: Supply, Demand & Order Flow
lessons.subtitle: Understanding the Battle Between Buyers and Sellers

steps.text: Supply zones are price levels where selling pressure overcomes buying pressure, causing price to reverse downward. In SMC, a supply zone is identified by a strong bearish move that breaks structure, with the zone mapped from the last bullish candle before the sell-off began. This is distinct from traditional supply and demand because SMC specifically ties the zone to the institutional Order Block. A supply zone is most valid when it contains a bearish OB at its origin. When price returns to a supply zone, look for signs of rejection to enter short.

Demand zones are the opposite: price levels where buying pressure overcomes selling pressure, causing price to reverse upward. A demand zone in SMC is mapped from the last bearish candle before a strong bullish move broke structure. It should contain a bullish OB. When price returns to a demand zone, look for a bullish reversal candle to enter long. The key difference between SMC demand and traditional demand is that SMC requires a clear structural break (BOS) following the zone to validate it. Without the BOS, the zone is just a random level, not institutional demand.

SMC redefines traditional supply and demand by anchoring it to market structure and Order Blocks. Traditional supply and demand zones are drawn based on consolidation areas and are often subjective. In SMC, a supply or demand zone is specifically the area containing the OB that preceded the structural break. This makes the zones more objective and repeatable. Additionally, SMC zones are always validated by a BOS in the opposite direction. If there is no BOS, there is no confirmed supply or demand zone. This stricter definition filters out many false signals.

The shift from supply to demand and vice versa is a critical concept. A zone that was previously strong supply can become demand if price breaks through it with momentum and returns to test it from above. This is called a supply-to-demand flip. For example, a resistance level that price breaks above and then returns to test from above becomes support. This flipping of zones is common in trending markets and gives you high-probability entry points. Always be aware that zones can change function. A level that worked as supply twice may act as demand the third time.

Imbalances in order flow are what create supply and demand zones. When there are more buyers than sellers at a given price, the order flow is imbalanced and price moves up to find more sellers. This imbalance leaves behind a zone of unfilled orders — the supply or demand zone. The size of the imbalance is reflected in the size of the candle that broke structure. A massive bullish BOS candle indicates a huge imbalance in buying pressure, making the demand zone behind it very significant. The larger the imbalance candle, the more powerful the zone.

High-probability zones have specific characteristics. First, they are formed on higher timeframes (4H or above). Second, they are preceded by a clear liquidity grab. Third, they contain a visible OB and FVG confluence. Fourth, the subsequent BOS candle is large and decisive. Fifth, the zone has not been tested more than once or twice. When you find a zone with all five characteristics, the probability of it holding on retest is very high. Focus your trading on these premium zones and avoid zones that lack these characteristics, as they are less likely to be defended by institutions.

Volume implications are often overlooked but valuable. In SMC, we do not rely on volume indicators directly, but we infer volume from price action. A gap or FVG implies very high volume at the time of formation because the market consumed all available orders instantly. Low-volume gaps within a supply or demand zone suggest that the zone is thin and may not hold well. High-volume zones (identified by the size of the breakout candle and the clarity of the OB) are much more likely to hold. The absence of overlapping wicks in the FVG tells you volume was extreme.

Combining supply and demand with market structure gives you a complete framework. Start with the daily chart: identify the overall structure (uptrend, downtrend, or range). Mark the major supply and demand zones on the daily. Move to the 4-hour chart: identify intermediate zones within the daily range. Finally, on the 1-hour chart: find the immediate supply or demand zone nearest to current price. Your trade direction is determined by the daily structure. Your entry is determined by the hourly supply or demand zone. This layered approach ensures you are trading with the institutional flow.

Practical exercise: Open a 4-hour chart of any major pair. Identify the last five significant moves that broke structure. For each move, find the OB that preceded it and mark that zone. Label it as supply (if the move was down) or demand (if the move was up). Now draw a rectangle covering the OB zone. Check how many of these zones have been retested and how they reacted. Count how many held and how many broke. This mapping exercise will show you that high-timeframe zones hold with high probability, while low-timeframe zones are less reliable.

Entry and exit strategies using supply and demand zones are straightforward. For a long entry: price enters a demand zone on the 1H/4H chart, shows a bullish rejection candle, and you enter with a stop below the zone. Target the next supply zone above. For a short entry: price enters a supply zone, shows a bearish rejection, enter short, stop above the zone, target the next demand zone below. If price breaks through your entry zone, exit immediately — the zone has failed and the structure has shifted. Never hold a trade hoping a broken zone will suddenly hold again.

lessons.title: Optimal Trade Entry — The Premium & Discount Concept
lessons.subtitle: Entering at the Best Possible Price Using Fibonacci

steps.text: The Premium and Discount concept divides any price move into two halves. The discount zone is the lower half (0% to 50% Fibonacci retracement), where price is considered cheap. The premium zone is the upper half (50% to 100% Fibonacci retracement), where price is considered expensive. Institutions buy in the discount zone and sell in the premium zone. Retail traders often do the opposite — they buy high (in premium) and sell low (in discount). Understanding this concept alone can transform your trading, as it forces you to wait for good prices rather than chasing moves.

To draw Fibonacci correctly in SMC, you must use the structural swing points. For a bullish retracement, identify a clear downtrend swing: a Lower High to a Lower Low. Draw the Fibonacci tool from the swing high (100%) to the swing low (0%). The discount zone is from 0% to 50%, and the premium zone is from 50% to 100%. For a bearish retracement, identify a clear uptrend swing: a Higher Low to a Higher High. Draw from swing low (0%) to swing high (100%). The discount zone for shorts is from 100% to 50% (the upper half), and premium is from 50% to 0% (the lower half).

The Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) zone in SMC is specifically the 70% to 80% retracement area within the premium/discount framework. For a long trade, the OTE zone is between 70% and 80% retracement of a downward swing, meaning price has pulled back significantly into the premium zone but not fully retraced. This is where institutions step in to buy because price has come down to a level where the risk-reward is favorable. For a short trade, the OTE zone is between 70% and 80% retracement of an upward swing, where price has rallied into the premium zone.

Why do institutions buy in discount and sell in premium? It is purely a matter of risk-reward. An institution buying at the 70% retracement of a swing has a stop-loss below the swing low (0%), a small distance away. Their target is the swing high (100%) or above, giving them a potential 3:1 or better risk-reward ratio. If they bought at the 50% level instead, their stop would need to be wider relative to the target, reducing the risk-reward. Institutions optimize for the best risk-reward, and the 70-80% zone offers the sweet spot. You should do the same.

Combining OTE with FVGs and Order Blocks creates the highest-probability entry setup in SMC. The sequence is: price makes a structural swing, then pulls back into the OTE zone (70-80%). Within the OTE zone, there should be an FVG and an Order Block at the same level. When all three align — OTE + FVG + OB — you have a confluence of three independent institutional signals. The probability of a reversal at this level is very high. This is the setup that professional traders scan for every day. Do not enter an OTE trade without at least one additional confluence factor.

Setting your stop-loss correctly is critical in OTE trading. The stop-loss should be placed just below the Order Block or Fair Value Gap that forms the lower boundary of your entry zone. Never place your stop at a round number or at the exact 100% Fibonacci level, as these are common hunting grounds for liquidity grabs. Instead, place it a few pips below the OB low for a long trade, or above the OB high for a short trade. This gives the trade enough room to breathe while protecting you from being stopped out by normal market noise.

Your take-profit target should be the next significant liquidity zone. For a long trade entered from the OTE zone, the target is the next swing high above. For a short trade, the target is the next swing low below. In trending markets, you can trail your stop as price moves in your favor, targeting multiple liquidity zones sequentially. A common approach is to take partial profits at the first target (50% of position) and let the rest run to the second or third target with a breakeven stop. This ensures you capture some profit even if the move does not reach the final target.

Risk-reward calculation in SMC is straightforward but must be done before entry. Calculate R (risk) as the distance from entry to stop-loss. Calculate the target as the distance from entry to the next liquidity zone. Divide the target distance by the risk distance. The result should be at least 2 (meaning 2:1 risk-reward). If it is less than 2, skip the trade no matter how perfect the setup looks. Disciplined risk-reward management is what separates professional traders from gamblers. Over many trades, a 2:1 risk-reward with a 50% win rate yields a net profit.

Example: EUR/USD on the 1-hour chart forms a clear downtrend swing from 1.1000 (high) to 1.0800 (low). Price starts pulling back. You draw Fibonacci from 1.1000 to 1.0800. The OTE zone is between 1.0940 and 1.0960 (70-80% retracement). Within this zone, you spot a bearish Order Block at 1.0950 and an FVG from 1.0945 to 1.0955. Price enters the zone and forms a bearish engulfing candle. You enter short at 1.0950, stop at 1.0965 (above the OB), target at 1.0800 (previous low). Risk = 15 pips, Reward = 150 pips — a 10:1 risk-reward. This is the kind of trade you want.

When OTE fails: sometimes price enters the 70-80% zone and continues straight through it, breaking past the 100% level. This is called an OTE failure or a sweep. When this happens, do not fight it. The institutional order flow was too strong and the retracement was not deep enough. Wait for price to break structure and form a new swing, then look for the OTE on the new swing. OTE failures often lead to powerful trending moves because they indicate strong momentum. If you get stopped out of an OTE trade, accept it and wait for the next setup. Never revenge trade after an OTE failure.

lessons.title: The Complete SMC Trading Plan
lessons.subtitle: From Analysis to Execution — Step by Step

steps.text: Step 1: Determine your bias from higher timeframe structure. Start with the daily chart. Identify whether the market is in an uptrend (Higher Highs and Higher Lows), a downtrend (Lower Highs and Lower Lows), or ranging. Your bias should match the daily structure. If the daily is in an uptrend, you should only look for long trades. If it is in a downtrend, only short trades. If it is ranging, wait for a breakout before committing. This single step will eliminate most of your losing trades because you will stop fighting the trend.

Step 2: Map key liquidity levels. On the 4-hour chart, identify the most recent swing high and swing low. Mark them with horizontal lines. These are your primary liquidity zones. Then identify the next swing levels beyond them. For an uptrend, the key liquidity levels are above the recent highs (buy-side liquidity). For a downtrend, the key levels are below the recent lows (sell-side liquidity). These levels are your potential targets and also the areas where liquidity grabs may occur. Without mapped liquidity levels, you are trading blind.

Step 3: Wait for a liquidity grab at a key level. Once you have your bias and mapped levels, let price come to one of those levels. Do not anticipate the move. If you are bullish on the daily, wait for price to drop toward a support level or previous low. Watch for a sharp spike below that level followed by an immediate reversal. That spike is the liquidity grab, hunting the stop-losses of traders who were long. The grab confirms that institutions are active at that level. Without this grab, the reversal is less reliable.

Step 4: Look for a CHoCH to confirm the reversal. After the liquidity grab, price should break structure in the opposite direction. In a bullish setup, price grabs liquidity below a low, then breaks above the recent Higher Low or swing low — a CHoCH to the upside. This confirms that the institutional move has begun. Do not enter on the liquidity grab alone; wait for the CHoCH. The grab is the trap, the CHoCH is the confirmation. If price grabs liquidity but does not produce a CHoCH, it was just a false breakout and the trend continues the other way.

Step 5: Identify your OTE zone (70-80% retracement). Draw Fibonacci from the most recent swing point. For a bullish setup, draw from the swing high (100%) to the swing low (0%) that was just made. The 70-80% retracement area is where you want price to return to for your entry. Mark this zone on your chart. If price does not reach this zone, do not chase it. If price goes beyond the 80% level, the setup is invalid and you need to redraw your Fibonacci on the new swing. Patience is essential — the OTE zone will come to price eventually.

Step 6: Find an OB + FVG confluence in the OTE zone. Within your marked OTE zone, look for a clear Order Block and/or Fair Value Gap. The OB should be the last candle before the aggressive move that formed the swing. The FVG should be the gap created by that aggressive move. When the OB and FVG overlap with the OTE zone, you have triple confluence. This is your trigger zone. Enter when price reaches this zone and forms a reversal candlestick pattern (engulfing, pin bar, or inside bar breakout). Do not enter before price actually touches this zone.

Step 7: Enter the trade with a stop-loss and take-profit. Entry: place your order at the OB/FVG level in the OTE zone after confirmation. Stop-loss: place it 5-10 pips below the OB low (for longs) or above the OB high (for shorts). Take-profit: set your first target at the next liquidity zone in the direction of the trade. For a long, that is the next swing high. For a short, the next swing low. Set a second target further out if the trend is strong. Always know your exact entry, stop, and target levels before you click the button.

Step 8: Manage the trade. Once the trade is running, do not watch it constantly. Set alerts at key levels. If price reaches your first target, take 50% of your position off the table and move your stop-loss to breakeven. If price continues, trail your stop behind each new structural level. For a long trade, trail the stop below each new Higher Low. For a short, trail above each new Lower High. If price reaches your second target, take another 25% off. Let the final 25% run with a wide stop. Trade management is what separates good traders from great ones.

Step 9: Review and journal the trade immediately after it closes. Write down: the setup (bias, liquidity grab, CHoCH, OTE, OB, FVG), the entry and exit prices, the risk-reward ratio, the outcome (win or loss), and most importantly how you felt during the trade. Did you follow the plan? Did you exit early? Did you move your stop emotionally? A trading journal is the fastest path to improvement. Review your journal weekly and look for patterns in your mistakes. Most traders make the same mistakes repeatedly until they write them down and consciously work to fix them.

Risk management rules are non-negotiable. Never risk more than 1-2% of your account on a single trade. If your account is $10,000, your maximum loss per trade is $100 to $200. This determines your position size. Never take more than 3 trades per day — after 3 losses, your judgment is compromised. Never add to a losing position. Never move your stop-loss away from price to give the trade more room. If the trade hits your stop, it was wrong. Accept the loss and wait for the next setup. These rules will keep you in the game long enough to become profitable.

Full worked example: EUR/USD daily chart shows an uptrend (HH/HL). 4H chart shows a swing low at 1.0800 and a swing high at 1.1000. Price drops to 1.0780, grabbing liquidity below 1.0800, then reverses to 1.0830. The break above 1.0800 is a CHoCH. Fibonacci drawn from 1.1000 to 1.0780 shows OTE at 1.0930-1.0960. Within that zone is an OB at 1.0940 and an FVG from 1.0935-1.0945. Price reaches 1.0945, forms a bearish engulfing on 15M. You enter short at 1.0945, stop at 1.0965 (above OB), target at 1.0800 (previous low). Risk 20 pips, reward 145 pips, R:R 7.25:1.

Final summary: SMC is a complete trading methodology, not a set of random tips. The framework is: higher timeframe bias determines direction. Liquidity levels tell you where price is heading. The liquidity grab is the trap, and the CHoCH is the confirmation. The OTE zone gives you the best entry price, and OB+FVG confluences increase probability. Risk management protects your capital. Reviewing your trades ensures continuous improvement. Commit to learning one concept at a time, practice it on a demo account, master it, then move to the next. Trading is a skill, not a lottery. Master the process and the profits will follow.
